summary:
Angie Jones recounts finding familiar developer flow state while building agents on a Friday night. She addresses the dread many engineers feel that AI agents are taking the fun parts of building, advising that the thrill moves up one layer to architecting agentic systems. The building blocks differ, but the engineering discipline remains the same. Using 'Relocation Scout,' a reusable house hunting agent, she walks through the engineering skills exercised during agent design.

Systems thinking means treating the agent as a component within a larger system with boundaries, dependencies, and failure modes. Workflow design gives agents a path, not just a goal; every run ends in stop, retry, or escalate. Decomposition addresses the agentic code smell of giant prompts, pulling apart distinct jobs. Separation of concerns places each responsibility in the right location: structured output in schemas, deterministic logic in scripts, meaty tasks in sub-agents, reusable processes as skills. Modularity extends this via reusable agent skills and sub-agents. Algorithmic thinking distinguishes tasks needing code (determinism) from tasks needing agents (judgment) from tasks needing humans (authority). Contracts and structured output ensure agent outputs are queryable and safe for downstream consumption.

State management and idempotency must handle retries and crashes, but model output variability introduces a trap where retries may look like new tasks. A lint pass can detect half-completed runs and retry only missing steps, relying on logged state. Threat modeling applies security engineering principles: validate inputs, grant least privilege, and draw boundaries around actions. Agent-consumed content from strangers must be treated as untrusted evidence, not instructions, and sensitive actions like emailing sellers or submitting offers should be walled behind human approval to reduce blast radius.

Maintainability is baked in through agent design files explaining workflows, policies, supporting resources, and memory upkeep, enabling any human or agent to orient in a fresh context without reverse-engineering prompts. Jones closes by affirming that designing agents is software engineering: the primitives differ, but the discipline of understanding systems, defining workflows, decomposing problems, managing state, designing for safety, and ensuring maintainability is unchanged. The joy of building has moved up a layer.

sections.title: Rediscovering engineering flow with agents
sections.summary: Angie Jones recounts finding familiar developer flow state while building agents on a Friday night. She addresses the dread some engineers feel about agents taking the fun parts, advising that the thrill moves up one layer to architecting agentic systems where the building blocks differ but the discipline is the same.

sections.title: Systems thinking: agent as component
sections.summary: Introduces Relocation Scout, a reusable house hunting agent. The first engineering skill is systems thinking: the agent is part of a larger system with files, tools, humans, and other agents. Jones argues against blindly letting coding agents build without first considering the agent's job, dependencies, boundaries, and failure modes.

sections.title: Workflow design: paths not just goals
sections.summary: The second skill is workflow design. Agents need a path, not just a goal. Every run ends in stop, retry, or escalate, and this path shapes architecture decisions about context, direct handling, and tool or person handoffs.

sections.title: Decomposition: splitting giant prompts
sections.summary: Giant prompts are the agentic equivalent of code smells, growing through edge cases, safety rules, and exceptions. Decomposition means spotting distinct jobs hidden in one blob and pulling them apart. Relocation Scout's prompt contains four jobs: normalizing listings, formatting shortlist, calculating commute, and researching neighborhood.

sections.title: Separation of concerns: right responsibility, right place
sections.summary: Separation of concerns places each responsibility in the right location. Listing normalization could become a skill, structured output defined in a schema, commute calculation in a boring script, and neighborhood research handled by a sub-agent, using the best tools for each job.

sections.title: Modularity: reusable agent capabilities
sections.summary: Modularity in agentic systems mirrors reusable functions and libraries. Skills can be reused across agents or shared like packages. Sub-agents are architecturally like functions with a specific scope, not carrying full session context. Judgment is needed to decide what is worth abstracting versus keeping local.

sections.title: Algorithmic thinking: code vs agent vs human
sections.summary: Algorithmic thinking distinguishes tasks best handled by code (exact answers, determinism) from tasks needing agents (judgment, ambiguity) from tasks needing humans (authority). Jones's rule: use code for determinism, agents for judgment, humans for authority. Ignoring this leads to unnecessarily complicated systems and inconsistent outputs.

sections.title: Contracts and structured output
sections.summary: When systems act on agent output, structured contracts are needed. Relocation Scout writes decisions with score, reason, and commute to structured memory using Compendium Wiki, enabling queryable persistence. This allows both human queries and downstream system steps to reliably consume agent output. Defining the shape forces clarity about what the agent should produce.

sections.title: State management and idempotency
sections.summary: Useful agentic systems must handle messy realities: duplicate webhooks, incomplete runs, retries. Agents must track state and design for idempotency. However, model output variability adds a trap where retries may reword requests enough to look like new tasks, making idempotency harder than in traditional software.

sections.title: Idempotency in practice: lint pass and partial retries
sections.summary: Jones illustrates idempotency with a concrete Relocation Scout scenario: the agent emails the realtor but crashes before blocking the calendar. A lint pass detects the incomplete run and retries only the missing calendar step, avoiding a duplicate email. This works because the agent checks what the system logged, completing only what is missing.

sections.title: Threat modeling: untrusted input and blast radius
sections.summary: Threat modeling applies security engineering fundamentals to agentic systems: validate inputs, grant least privilege, and draw boundaries around what actions can touch. Relocation Scout consumes listing copy, forum threads, and reviews from strangers, all treated as untrusted evidence, not instructions. Sensitive actions like emailing sellers, booking tours, or submitting offers are walled behind human approval, reducing blast radius and minimizing risk exposure.

sections.title: Maintainability: agent design files and cold starts
sections.summary: Jones avoids letting coding agents design other agents because the result may technically work but be unmaintainable. Instead, she bakes maintainability into every system level via an agent design file explaining the workflow, policy locations, supporting resources (skills, scripts, sub-agents), and memory upkeep. The test is whether a fresh context can jump in cold and know exactly what to do. When modifications fail, that signals maintainability needs improvement.

sections.title: Closing: designing agents is software engineering
sections.summary: Jones closes by affirming that designing agents is software engineering. The primitives are different, but the discipline is the same: understand the system, define workflows, decompose problems, place responsibilities correctly, make things reusable, choose the right actors, define contracts, manage state, design for safety, and make the system understandable. The thrill of building remains; it has just moved up a layer.

demonstrations: Relocation Scout: a reusable house hunting agent that pulls listings, weighs neighborhood signals, and returns a ranked short list

Mapping responsibilities to components: listing normalization as a skill, commute calculation as a script, neighborhood research as a sub-agent, shortlist format as a schema
Using Compendium Wiki as an agent memory layer with structured fields (decision, score, reason)

Giant prompts cause agents to drift and not stick to the script
